text: You checked the first four and last four characters, they matched, and the money still went to a scammer.
So what did you miss? It wasn't really your address. It was a lookalike, planted in your own history.
Imagine paying a friend back with the address you copied last week.
A wallet address is a long string of characters. Most people skip the middle.
A scammer's computer churns out addresses until one starts and ends like yours.
Then it sends you a tiny amount, often zero, from the lookalike.
Now it sits in your history, beside the real one.
Next time, you copy the top one. The ends match. The middle never did.
Once it's sent, no bank can pull it back.
In May 2024, someone sent a small test, then about sixty-eight million dollars to a lookalike.
It was returned after a negotiation. That campaign had over eighty-two thousand lookalikes.
That's also why strangers send you tiny or zero amounts. Never copy those.
And it's why the three dots in a shortened address hide exactly what's different.
And it's why paying a saved contact, username or QR code beats pasting.
So nobody broke into your wallet. You checked the ends, they matched, and you sent it yourself.
Follow me, and send this to someone who only checks the first and last few characters.
